what_its_for: Rifabutin is an antibiotic used to prevent or treat a serious bacterial infection called Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC). This infection most often affects people with HIV/AIDS who have weakened immune systems. It may also be used along with other medicines to treat tuberculosis (TB).
how_to_take: Take rifabutin by mouth, usually once a day. You can take it with or without food. If the medicine upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. If you have trouble swallowing the capsule, you can open it and mix the powder with applesauce. Do not skip doses, even if you feel well. Take the full course of medicine as your doctor prescribed.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg once a day. Your doctor may split this into 150 mg twice a day if the medicine upsets your stomach. Your dose may be different if you take certain other medicines (such as antifungals or HIV drugs), or if you have kidney or liver problems. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. But if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store rifabutin capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed and away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine that is expired — check the date on the bottle and safely dispose of old medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking rifabutin with certain medicines without your doctor's approval, especially antifungals (like fluconazole or voriconazole), some HIV medicines, and blood thinners. Do not drink large amounts of alcohol while taking this medicine. Be aware that rifabutin can turn your urine, saliva, sweat, tears, and skin a reddish-orange or brownish color — this is normal and harmless, but it can permanently stain contact lenses, so avoid wearing soft contact lenses. Rifabutin can make hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings) less effective — use a backup method like condoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems), severe stomach pain or nausea, vision changes or eye pain (possible uveitis — eye inflammation), muscle pain or weakness, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever, chills, or signs of a new infection, a skin rash or allergic reaction (hives, swelling, trouble breathing), or numbness or tingling in your hands or feet. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: Rifabutin starts working right away to fight bacteria, but you may not feel different for several weeks. For MAC prevention, you will usually take it for a long time — sometimes indefinitely — as long as your immune system remains weak. For treating an active infection, continue taking it for as long as your doctor directs, even if you feel better. Stopping too early can allow the bacteria to come back or become resistant to the medicine.
special_populations: Older adults: No special dose is usually needed, but your doctor will monitor you more closely for side effects. Kidney problems: If you have severe kidney disease, your doctor may lower your dose. Liver problems: Use with caution. Your doctor may run blood tests to check your liver while you take this medicine. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking rifabutin if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Children: Rifabutin can be used in children with HIV/AIDS, but the dose will be calculated based on your child's weight. Always follow the pediatrician's instructions. Breastfeeding: It is not known if rifabutin passes into breast milk. Women with HIV are generally advised not to breastfeed. Ask your doctor for guidance.
